name: Securities Act
location: Building a Fraud Risk Management Program, FTX case example, pp. 11–12
focus: Anti-fraud provisions relating to representations made to investors.
exam: False statements about safety, controls, or compliance used to attract investors can support securities-fraud charges.
trap: The guide mentions this in the FTX case; it is not part of the main regional-law comparison table.

name: Securities Exchange Act
location: Building a Fraud Risk Management Program, FTX case example, pp. 11–12
focus: Anti-fraud provisions relevant to securities markets and investor deception.
exam: Pair it with the Securities Act in the FTX case: false investor representations and concealed risks.
trap: Do not confuse the law with the Securities and Exchange Commission, which is the regulator.

name: Sarbanes-Oxley Act
location: Building a Fraud Risk Management Program, US anti-fraud regulations, p. 24
focus: Corporate governance and financial reporting for public companies.
exam: Requires strong internal controls, accurate financial records, and reporting of internal-control weaknesses.
trap: SOX is about governance, controls, and reporting—not consumer reimbursement for electronic fraud.

name: Electronic Fund Transfer Act / Regulation E
location: Building a Fraud Risk Management Program, pp. 24–25 and 93–94
focus: Consumer protection for electronic payments and unauthorized transactions.
exam: Investigate unauthorized transactions; use account blocking and payment recalls where appropriate. The guide states 10 days without provisional credit and 45–90 days with provisional credit, depending on criteria.
trap: Reg E is the electronic-payments rule; do not confuse it with SOX or securities regulation.

name: Dodd-Frank Act
location: Building a Fraud Risk Management Program, US anti-fraud regulations, p. 25
focus: Whistleblower protection and measures to detect and prevent financial fraud.
exam: The fastest association is Dodd-Frank = whistleblower protections.
trap: The guide does not present it as the electronic-payment reimbursement law.

name: Foreign Corrupt Practices Act
location: Building a Fraud Risk Management Program, US anti-fraud regulations, p. 25
focus: Corporate fraud risk involving bribery of foreign officials.
exam: FCPA = prohibition on bribery of foreign public officials.
trap: Do not confuse bribery and corruption risk with ordinary payment fraud or identity theft.

name: Fair Credit Reporting Act
location: Building a Fraud Risk Management Program, Fraud investigation sources, p. 78
focus: Collection, access, and distribution of consumer credit-reporting data.
exam: During investigations, senior managers must understand rights and responsibilities governing consumer-data use.
trap: FCRA governs consumer-reporting data; it is not the same as GDPR’s broader EU personal-data framework.

name: General Data Protection Regulation
location: Building a Fraud Risk Management Program, EU anti-fraud regulations, p. 25
focus: Protection of personal data and privacy.
exam: Strict requirements for data collection, processing, storage, privacy, and security; cross-border transfers may require equivalent protection.
trap: GDPR is a data-protection law, while MAR targets market abuse and PSD2 targets payment services.

name: Market Abuse Regulation
location: Building a Fraud Risk Management Program, EU anti-fraud regulations, pp. 25–26
focus: Transparency and fairness in financial markets.
exam: Prevents insider trading and market manipulation and supports equal access to information.
trap: MAR is not the EU payments-security rule; that is PSD2.

name: Revised Payment Services Directive
location: Building a Fraud Risk Management Program, EU anti-fraud regulations, p. 26
exam: Secure Customer Authentication, open banking, licensing rules, and transparency in payment services.
trap: PSD2 is the EU directive; the UK adopted it through the Payment Services Regulations.

name: Fraud Act
location: Building a Fraud Risk Management Program, UK anti-fraud regulations, pp. 26–27
exam: Three offences: false representation, failure to disclose information, and abuse of position. Core elements are dishonesty plus intent to gain or cause loss/risk of loss.
trap: Do not confuse the Fraud Act’s substantive offences with ECCTA’s corporate failure-to-prevent offence.

name: Payment Services Regulations
location: Building a Fraud Risk Management Program, UK anti-fraud regulations, pp. 26–27
exam: Strong Customer Authentication, refund for unauthorized transactions by the end of the next business day, and Confirmation of Payee.
trap: The study guide uses PSR for the regulations and also discusses the Payment Systems Regulator as a body—do not mix them.

name: Economic Crime and Corporate Transparency Act
location: Building a Fraud Risk Management Program, UK anti-fraud regulations, p. 27
exam: An organization can be liable when an employee or agent commits fraud benefiting it and reasonable fraud-prevention procedures are absent.
trap: Focus on organizational liability and reasonable prevention procedures.

name: Financial Services and Markets Act
location: Building a Fraud Risk Management Program, UK anti-fraud regulations, pp. 26–27
focus: Legal basis for APP-scam reimbursement regimes.
exam: Memorize the guide’s figures: 50/50 split between sending and receiving PSPs; £85,000 cap; reimbursement within five business days in most cases; customer may bear up to £100.
trap: FSMA provides the legal basis; the Payment Systems Regulator publishes the detailed APP reimbursement requirements.

name: Proceeds of Crime Act 2002
location: Fraud Investigations, When do you have enough evidence?, p. 87
focus: Asset recovery and freezing considerations during investigation closure.
exam: Before closing, assess whether sufficient grounds exist for asset recovery or freezing under POCA or a similar legal framework.
trap: The guide mentions POCA in the evidence-and-case-closure context, not in the main UK fraud-law comparison.

name: Criminal Code Act
location: Building a Fraud Risk Management Program, region-specific regulations, p. 28
focus: Fraud offences including obtaining property or financial advantage by deception and fraudulent money transfers.
exam: The guide states prison terms can be as long as 10 years.
trap: Keep Australia’s 10-year figure separate from Canada’s thresholds.

name: Criminal Code of Canada
location: Building a Fraud Risk Management Program, region-specific regulations, p. 28
focus: Fraud offences including mail, stock-exchange, insider-trading, document-falsification, and identity-theft fraud.
exam: More than CA$5,000: maximum 14 years. Less than CA$5,000: maximum 2 years.
trap: Canada is the jurisdiction with the CA$5,000 threshold distinction.

name: Criminal Law of China
location: Building a Fraud Risk Management Program, region-specific regulations, p. 28
focus: Defines fraudulent actions and establishes penalties.
exam: The guide states a maximum of five years’ imprisonment for basic fraud.
trap: China is the five-year figure in the regional comparison.

name: Penal Code
location: Building a Fraud Risk Management Program, region-specific regulations, p. 28
exam: Maximum 10 years; related offences include computer fraud, breach of trust, and securities fraud.
trap: Japan and Australia both carry a 10-year maximum in the guide, but the listed offence details differ.
